name: Bordeaux & Bordeaux Supérieur

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, warm summer

climate: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Sémillon sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.

terms: France's protected place names. A wine sold under one must follow that appellation's rules. The EU's term for the same tier is PDO, or AOP in French.
Indication Géographique Protégée, the tier below AOC. It replaced vin de pays in 2009.
France's simplest category, in use since 2010. It replaced vin de table.
There is no legal or agreed definition of old, so the words promise nothing on their own.
One of the two regional appellations allowed anywhere in Bordeaux, beside plain Bordeaux. Together they cover about half the Bordeaux vineyard.

In 1855 brokers ranked Bordeaux estates by reputation and price. Reds were ranked from first to fifth growths, nearly all in the Médoc, and the sweet whites of Sauternes and Barsac from superior first growth to second growth.

notes: Plain Bordeaux AOC wines are fruity, with little oak, and are made to drink young.

blurb.text: A grouping within Bordeaux that holds the Bordeaux Supérieur appellation. Bordeaux's rules allow Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cot, Carmenère and Petit Verdot for red, plus Sauvignon, Sémillon and Muscadelle. The Gironde area grows mostly Merlot (58 percent) and Cabernet Sauvignon (20).
